p.x:
Last weekend, my class went to Sukhothai, an old town in the north of Thailand. More than 700 years ago, it was the capital of a Thai kingdom. A famous king, King Ramkhamhaeng, ruled there in the 13th century. Our teacher told us that he created the first Thai alphabet. For many Thais, he is a national hero.
We rode bicycles around the ancient city. There were old temples, a big wall and beautiful lakes with lotus flowers. In the afternoon, we visited the museum. We saw old pots, coins and a stone with ancient writing on it. I tried to read it, but it was very difficult!
Our guide said that Sukhothai means "the dawn of happiness". In the past, it was a peaceful place where people traded and farmed. It was strange to think that people lived there so long ago. I learned more about history in one day than in a whole term at school!

p.t: The Rise and Fall of Ayutthaya
p.x:
For more than four hundred years, from 1351 to 1767, Ayutthaya was one of the richest cities in Asia. It was the centre of a powerful kingdom, and at its height it controlled an area almost as large as an empire. European explorers who visited in the 17th century described it as more beautiful than London or Paris. Merchants from China, Japan, Persia and Europe came to trade, and many foreigners became citizens of the city.
Ayutthaya fought many wars with its neighbours. The most famous battle took place in 1767, when the Burmese army destroyed the city after a long siege. Many temples were burned, and thousands of people were taken away. According to legend, the city's treasures were hidden in secret places, but nobody has ever found them.
However, the nation did not disappear. Within a few months, King Taksin gathered an army and won back independence. Today, the ruins of Ayutthaya are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Historians continue to study the old records, and visitors come from all over the world to see the famous statue of a Buddha's head trapped in the roots of a tree.

Much of what we know about early human history comes not from written records but from the work of archaeologists. By carefully excavating ancient sites, they uncover artefacts such as tools, pottery and jewellery that reveal how people lived thousands of years ago. At Ban Chiang in north-eastern Thailand, for example, excavations revealed painted pottery and bronze objects suggesting that a sophisticated civilisation existed there more than 3,000 years ago.
Dating these finds is crucial. Scientists use methods such as radiocarbon dating to place an object within a particular era. Written evidence, when it exists, adds further detail: records of a king's reign, for instance, help historians link archaeological layers to specific dynasties.
Yet the past is often more complicated than textbooks suggest. In medieval Europe and Asia alike, a single invasion could wipe out a city, while a peace treaty might reshape borders for centuries. Many great monuments survive only because they were forgotten, buried under sand or jungle, and later rediscovered.
Today, archaeology faces new challenges. Construction projects threaten unexcavated sites, and illegal trade in stolen artefacts remains a serious problem. Many experts argue that protecting these sites is not just about the past: it is about preserving a shared human story for future generations.
